/static/books/aleph.jpg.notes: Jorge Luis Borges is something else. Borges' power to hold out what the true meaning is, who the character is, and what their purpose is right up until the last page, often the last sentence, is what makes me so captivated by him. His choice to write from antagonists, through the eyes of the enemy, was a bit curious to me to start with, but I truly came to appreciate it with "Deutsches Requiem". Borges doesn't sympathize with the protagonist, but rather uses him as a metonym for nazism, the way he thinks is illogical and nonsensical. Borges' works in this collection are fantastic, it is nice to let yourself be enveloped by story after story, even if for just a few pages at a time.
/static/books/aleph.jpg.title: The Aleph and Other Stories / Jorge Luis Borges

/static/books/crying_of_lot.jpg.notes: Some of the best character names ever, and highly relevant to modern American culture. Would love to read this again as soon as possible, likely the most dense 150 pages I’ve ever read.

/static/books/giovanni.jpg.notes: So fantastically written that you feel the heartbreak in every word on the page. Baldwin tells us that as humans we exist to give love, through whatever medium possible. I don't think any review of this book can do it justice, Baldwin is a pure embodiment of what every author should strive to be. Contains what I think is one of the most beautiful lines ever written "I loved her as much as ever and I still didn't know how much that was."
/static/books/giovanni.jpg.title: Giovanni's Room / James Baldwin

/static/books/if_on_a_winter_night.jpg.notes: I was recommended this by an older gentleman in a bookshop who told me that it would be one of the greatest books I’ve ever read. He was right. Calvino creates ten distinct realities, each interpolated in a narration that I lived through. I’d never seen the use of second person to describe the main character, and his references to him (or sometimes her) captured me more than I could have imagined. In many ways, reading this feels like a deep meditation, a narrator lead me through an imaginary tale, pushing me to discover an inner meaning along the way. This book enveloped me in its pages, I truly felt like the "you" that Calvino constantly refers to in alternating chapters of this book. Since reading, I have become a die-hard Calvino fan. I owe a lot to the man in the bookstore.
/static/books/if_on_a_winter_night.jpg.title: If On a Winter's Night a Traveler / Italo Calvino

/static/books/left_bank.jpg.notes: I read this in a week where I genuinely felt the fear, excitement, joy, and craze of living ten years in the Left Bank. I learned so much about the livelihoods of writers, artists, and musicians I love, and much more about those I've never heard of. The messy yet beautiful landscape of politics, friendship, and sex Poirier contends with here feels like watching a perfect dumpster fire. Recommend to all, haven't been so captivated by a book in ages.
/static/books/left_bank.jpg.title: Left Bank: Art, Passion, and the Rebirth of Paris, 1940-50 / Agnès Poirier

/static/books/letters_to_young_poet.jpg.notes: My mom gifted me this book before I went to college, and I finally came around to reading it a little into my second semester, serving as a really beautiful guiding point in grounding myself and understanding who I want to be. Rilke's manner of speech is so clear, so fluid, and so immensely insightful, that I found myself reading this cover to cover in one sitting. In his letters he conveys the benefits of being confused, importance of being lost, and the power of being alone. I will always cherish Rilke’s ability to witness things not for their ugliness but for their beauty.
/static/books/letters_to_young_poet.jpg.title: Letters to a Young Poet / Rainer Maria Rilke

/static/books/must_change_life.jpg.notes:
Rodin’s and Rilke’s lives flow with such artistic vision and passion, with unknown greatness, with an oxymoronic conceited humility. These two men, incredibly different in their personal natures, somehow came to find each other in this world, somehow came to establish themselves as masters, came to be the angels and demons they wrote and sculpted of. Rodin was Rilke's greatest teacher, greatest influence, his God, and Rilke was Rodin's greatest listener, his greatest amicable failure, his final friend even in their falling out. The two men share an inexplicable bond, one unfathomable to those that walk this earth. A man who was too self-indulgent to notice death creeping up behind him and a man who was too self-aware to ever fear death itself. A man killed by disease that he fought to avoid and a man killed by the beauty of nature that he sought to rewrite as the futile life before death. A man who involuntarily confronted death in fear and loneliness and a man who voluntarily endured death in solitude and strength. The story of Rodin and Rilke, of mentor and mentee, of friends and at times enemies, reads as a fable. These men, polar opposites in many ways and the most unlikely of companions, coexisted unlike any have before. 
"And people say that Puvis de Chavannes is not a fine artist!" 
"Rose, O pure contradiction, desire to be no one's sleep beneath so many lids."
/static/books/must_change_life.jpg.title: You Must Change Your Life: The Story of Rainer Maria Rilke and Auguste Rodin / Rachel Corbett

/static/books/notebooks_of_malte.jpg.notes: Rilke’s words create frames for the reader to see the world and themselves. He creates not just paintings here, but mirrors as well.

/static/film/arrebato.jpg.notes:
Rather than a religious rapture, here Zulueta explores an existential and metaphysical rapture. First, he questions if all humans have a natural purpose on this earth, in our physical world, as Pedro, his clear alter ego, comes to question. Pedro believes that his life is not behind the camera, but inside of it. Film defines his destiny. Second, the film poses an ontological question: do the images of objects represented in cinema exist in the same ontological reality as those that exist outside the filmic world? Zulueta clearly answers No. He aims to communicate to his audience that cinema is a new dimension, it is a world outside of ours, the images and objects shown in it have completely altered forms, they are not the same. 
 Heroin fulfills the function of a vampire who absorbs José's quotidian life and robs the fun from his sexual one. For Pedro, heroin provides a state of recluse, but allows him to communicate with those around him confidently, even if briefly. When he discovers his first "arrebato," Pedro becomes addicted to the camera and its ability to act as a vampire, absorbing his life force. This parallel is not purely metaphoric; throughout the film, two things draw blood: the heroin needle and the camera. In the first of his films of rapture, a red frame is interspliced, increasing with frequency as Pedro endures more and more outbursts. Just as a vampire sucks the blood dry from a human, here the camera sucks Pedro’s natural, earthly life force until he is one with the tape. 
 And, as a newly converted vampire must, Pedro needs a victim. This victim is José. The camera is a vampire that converts Pedro, and Pedro is a vampire that must convert José.
/static/film/arrebato.jpg.title: Arrebato / Iván Zulueta
